title: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement and repealing Directive 2004/18/EC
summary: The core EU public procurement directive governing contract awards by public authorities. It explicitly authorises life-cycle costing, environmental award criteria, technical specifications referencing eco-labels, and reserved contracts, letting authorities demand recycled content, durability and repairability rather than awarding on lowest price alone. This turns roughly 14% of EU GDP in public spending into demand-side pull for circular products and services. It is the legal backbone that EU Green Public Procurement criteria plug into.

title: Directive 2014/25/EU on procurement by entities operating in the water, energy, transport and postal services sectors and repealing Directive 2004/17/EC
summary: The utilities counterpart to 2014/24/EU, covering procurement by network operators in water, energy, transport and postal sectors. It carries the same green levers: life-cycle costing, environmental technical specifications and award criteria, enabling utilities to require recycled content, resource efficiency and end-of-life performance in high-volume infrastructure purchasing. Because utilities buy long-lived capital goods, its circular-economy reach is material-intensive and durable.

title: Directive (EU) 2019/1161 amending Directive 2009/33/EC on the promotion of clean and energy-efficient road transport vehicles
summary: Sets binding minimum public-procurement targets for clean and zero-emission vehicles that Member States' authorities must meet when buying or leasing road transport and contracting bus/waste-collection services. It uses public purchasing power as a mandated market-creation lever for low-impact fleets. As a procurement mandate it enables the circular/low-carbon transition on the demand side rather than through emissions limits on manufacturers.

title: Directive (EU) 2024/1799 on common rules promoting the repair of goods
summary: The EU 'Right to Repair' directive. It obliges manufacturers to repair products covered by repairability requirements even beyond the legal guarantee period, bars contractual/technical/software barriers that block independent repair or use of second-hand and 3D-printed spare parts, and creates a European repair information platform plus a standard European Repair Information Form. The mechanism extends product lifespans and builds an independent repair market, directly displacing premature replacement.

title: Directive (EU) 2024/825 amending Directives 2005/29/EC and 2011/83/EU as regards empowering consumers for the green transition
summary: Amends EU consumer-protection law to ban greenwashing and, crucially for circularity, to outlaw practices that induce premature obsolescence and to require pre-contract disclosure of product durability and repairability (a harmonised repairability score and guarantee information). By forcing repairability and lifespan information at the point of sale and prohibiting designed-in early failure, it steers demand toward durable, repairable goods. It works as the information-and-obsolescence complement to the Right to Repair Directive.

title: A new Circular Economy Action Plan: For a cleaner and more competitive Europe (COM(2020) 98 final)
summary: The European Commission's flagship circular-economy strategy under the Green Deal. It is the framework roadmap that launched the sustainable-products initiative, the right-to-repair agenda, packaging and plastics reforms, and sector plans for electronics, batteries, textiles and construction. Although a Communication rather than binding law, it is the policy scaffolding under which ESPR, PPWR and the Right to Repair Directive were subsequently adopted, and it sets the EU's circular targets and priorities.

title: Directive 2008/98/EC on waste and repealing certain Directives (Waste Framework Directive)
summary: The base Waste Framework Directive that establishes the five-step waste hierarchy (prevention, preparing for re-use, recycling, other recovery, disposal), the definitions of waste/by-product/end-of-waste, and the general minimum requirements for extended producer responsibility schemes and recycling targets. It is the foundational legal architecture on which EU recycling and EPR law is built. Distinct from the 2018/852 packaging amendment already in the corpus; note it is itself amended by Directive (EU) 2018/851.

title: Regulation (EU) 2021/783 establishing a Programme for the Environment and Climate Action (LIFE) 2021-2027
summary: Establishes the LIFE programme, the EU's dedicated funding instrument for environment and climate action, with a EUR 5.4 billion budget for 2021-2027 including a 'Circular Economy and Quality of Life' sub-programme. It provides grants and co-financing for circular-economy pilots, waste-prevention, recycling infrastructure and eco-innovation projects. The mechanism is direct financial support that de-risks and scales circular business models and public initiatives.

title: Regulation (EU) 2020/852 on the establishment of a framework to facilitate sustainable investment (EU Taxonomy)
summary: Creates the EU classification system for environmentally sustainable economic activities, with 'transition to a circular economy' as one of its six defined environmental objectives. By setting technical screening criteria that investments must meet to be labelled sustainable, it channels private capital and disclosure obligations toward circular activities such as recycling, re-use, durable design and secondary-raw-material use. The lever is financial: it steers investment flows rather than mandating product behaviour.

title: Procurement Act 2023
summary: Overhauls UK public procurement post-Brexit, replacing the EU-derived regime. It lets contracting authorities set award criteria and conditions tied to public benefit, including environmental and circular-economy considerations, and requires regard to national procurement policy priorities. This makes public purchasing a demand-side lever for recycled content, whole-life value and waste reduction across UK public spending. It is the primary UK statute giving legal footing to green/circular procurement.

title: Environment Act 2021
summary: The UK's post-Brexit environmental framework statute. It provides the enabling powers for the whole modern UK circular-economy toolkit: extended producer responsibility for packaging, deposit return schemes, consistent household/business recycling collections, resource-efficiency and eco-design information requirements, and charges on single-use items. It also creates legally binding long-term environmental targets and the Office for Environmental Protection. It is the parent framework under which most UK circular secondary legislation is made.

title: The Ecodesign for Energy-Related Products and Energy Information Regulations 2021
summary: The UK's 'right to repair' regulations. They impose ecodesign requirements on categories of energy-related products (including refrigeration, washing machines, dishwashers, electric motors and displays) that mandate availability of spare parts to professional repairers for up to 7-10 years, access to repair and maintenance information, and design allowing disassembly with common tools. The mechanism forces repairability and spare-part supply into product design, extending appliance lifespans. It is the UK analogue to the EU ecodesign/right-to-repair regime.

title: The Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations 2013
summary: The UK's extended producer responsibility regime for electrical and electronic equipment, transposing (and now retaining) EU Directive 2012/19/EU. Producers must register, finance the collection, treatment and recycling of WEEE, meet recovery/recycling targets, and fund take-back, while distributors provide collection points. The mechanism internalises end-of-life costs and builds e-waste recycling infrastructure, keeping electronics materials in circulation. It is the flagship UK EPR scheme for electronics.

title: The Producer Responsibility Obligations (Packaging and Packaging Waste) Regulations 2024
summary: The UK's modernised packaging extended producer responsibility scheme, made under the Environment Act 2021 and replacing the old PRN-based 2007 regime. Producers must register, report packaging placed on the market, pay fees calculated on an eco-modulated recyclability basis, and cover the full net cost of managing packaging waste collected by local authorities. The fee mechanism rewards recyclable, minimal packaging and funds recycling infrastructure, shifting cost from taxpayers to producers. It is the current cornerstone of UK packaging circularity.

title: The Deposit and Return Scheme for Scotland Regulations 2020
summary: Establishes a deposit return scheme in Scotland for single-use drinks containers in PET plastic, glass, aluminium and steel, requiring a refundable deposit that consumers reclaim on return. The financial deposit lever drives high-quality separate collection and closed-loop recycling of beverage containers, cutting litter and boosting recycled-content feedstock. Launch was repeatedly deferred and later aligned to a UK-wide 2027 scheme, but the Regulations remain the enacted statutory basis.

title: The Waste (England and Wales) Regulations 2011
summary: Transposes and retains the EU Waste Framework Directive (2008/98/EC, as amended by 2018/851) for England and Wales. It embeds the waste hierarchy into UK law, requires businesses to apply prevention/re-use/recycling in that order, mandates separate collection of key recyclable streams, and underpins duty-of-care and waste-carrier controls. It is the framework statute translating EU circular waste principles into operative UK obligations.

title: Finance Act 2021 (Part 2, Plastic Packaging Tax)
summary: Part 2 of the Finance Act 2021 creates the UK Plastic Packaging Tax, a per-tonne charge on plastic packaging manufactured in or imported into the UK that contains less than 30% recycled plastic. The tax is a financial lever that makes virgin plastic more expensive relative to recycled content, directly incentivising manufacturers to design in recycled material and pulling demand through the recycling value chain. It is one of the UK's clearest fiscal circular-economy instruments.
